newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa-China trade may surge after Taiwan move.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa-China trade may surge after Taiwan move.

text.p: South African trade with China is likely to soar after Pretoria's decision to recognise Beijing and cut diplomatic ties with Taiwan, politicians and trade officials said on Thursday.
"This will be a great spur for trade between South Africa and the People's Republic of China," said Raymond Suttner, chairman of parliament's foreign affairs committee.

Taiwan is South Africa's seventh-largest trading partner with trade totalling 5.7 billion rand ($1.25 billion) in 1995 while that with China and Hong Kong combined was 6.2 billion rand, according to the South African Foreign Trade Organisation.

Trade with mainland China has increased about 200 percent since the early 1990s. It rose by 47 percent in 1995 alone and was likely to continue climbing, the trade organisation's spokeswoman Liz Whitehouse said.
President Nelson Mandela told reporters in Johannesburg on Wednesday that Pretoria would switch diplomatic recognition from Taipei to Beijing by the end of 1997.
Suttner said China's rulers were more directly involved in its economy than most governments in capitalist countries.
"Not having diplomatic relations is a barrier to economic relations, so diplomatic relations will certainly facilitate our economic relations with Beijing," he added.
Whitehouse said Pretoria's decision to ditch Taiwan -- a diplomatic ally which stood by the previous white-minority government during the apartheid years -- should not affect trade.
"The decision to cut diplomatic ties with Taiwan should not have too much impact on our trade," Whitehouse said.
South Africa's exports to Taiwan were mainly minerals and metals, Whitehouse said, adding: "Certainly there will still be a need for those products from South Africa."
Taiwan said on Thursday it would continue buying coal and uranium from South Africa but the island's government said it would not continue to encourage investments.

"Without government encouragement, it will be hard (for private investments) to proceed there," Chiang Ping-kun, chairman of the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development said when asked whether a US$3 billion petrochemical project by Taiwan's Tuntex Distinct Corp would continue.
But South Africa's Trade and Industry ministry said investments were unlikely to be affected because business principles usually won over politics.

"This should not affect our economic relations. It is our responsibility now to ensure the smooth transition (from Taiwan to China) that the president speaks of," Trade and Industry spokesman Ismail Lagardien said.
"Ultimately our economic relations are business to business and people to people."

South Africa is the biggest of 30 countries -- mostly underdeveloped states in Central America and Africa -- which recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government rather than the communist government on the mainland.
Taiwan and China have been separated since a civil war ended in 1949.
China sees Taiwan as a renegade province not entitled to foreign ties while Taiwan insists its 21 million people have a right not to be excluded from international activities. ($1=4.56 rand)
